notes.title: What a checkpoint contains, and how often you take one

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Checkpoint per super-step, keyed by thread, with resume from the last one — LangGraph: persistence

  • Durable execution as a workflow-engine primitive rather than something you build — Temporal: what is durable execution

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Durable Execution — Checkpointing, HITL Interrupts, Time Travel — the mechanism and what a framework provides.

  • State Management — checkpoints keyed to a thread id.

  • statefulness and persistence — where state lives in a production agent.

What this note adds: the two choices those notes leave open — what goes in the checkpoint, and where the boundaries are. Both are cost-versus-recovery trades, and both are where "we use a checkpointer" stops being an answer.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The framing that scores? This is a workflow-engine problem, not a novel agent problem.
What goes in a checkpoint? Everything needed to resume — and nothing re-derivable.
Where's the boundary? After a side effect, always. That's what makes resume safe.
The cost knob? Checkpoint frequency × payload size, written on the hot path.
What a checkpoint is not? An audit log. Different retention, different readers.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

Checkpointing an agent is the same problem as durable workflow execution, and saying that early is worth doing because it moves the conversation onto ground where the answers are known. Two decisions matter. What's in the checkpoint: enough to resume, and nothing that can be re-derived, because payload size is paid on every step. And where the boundaries fall: always immediately after a side effect, so a crash can't replay a write. Get the second wrong and resume becomes a duplicate-effect generator, which is worse than not resuming at all.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
No checkpointing Runs are short, synchronous and cheap to redo. A crash loses the run; no HITL, no long runs. Seconds-long request/response.
Checkpoint per step, full state Default for long runs. Simplest to reason about. Write per step; payload grows with accumulated state. Runs measured in minutes; resume matters.
Checkpoint per step, delta State is large and mostly unchanged between steps. Reconstruction complexity; a corrupt delta breaks the chain. Large documents carried in state.
Checkpoint at side-effect boundaries only Writes are rare; most steps are pure reads. A crash mid-read-sequence redoes those reads. Long read phases punctuated by occasional writes.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
None No store. Runs are ephemeral. Nothing. A pod eviction is a lost run, and nothing counts it.
Per-step full A durable store keyed by thread id, written on the hot path. One write per step; latency added to every step. Checkpoint size is a metric; schema changes need migration.
Per-step delta Store plus a reconstruction path. Smaller writes; CPU on restore. Chain integrity becomes a failure mode of its own.
Boundary-only Fewer, larger writes at semantically meaningful points. Cheaper steady state; more rework on crash. You must know which steps have effects — the read/write split again.

The redraw test: checkpointing puts a durable store next to the loop and makes resume an arrow back into a named step. If the diagram has a loop and no store, the run is ephemeral whatever the brief said.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

The payload trade. Checkpoint cost is roughly frequency × payload. A 200 KB state written every step for twelve steps is 2.4 MB per run, on the hot path, before the store's own latency. That's the argument for keeping large artifacts out of the checkpoint and holding references instead — which is the same offloading decision as §5's context budget, arriving from the durability side.

Recovery arithmetic. If a step costs c and a run is n steps, a crash at step k costs k × c without checkpointing and roughly one step with it. For a twelve-step run failing at step ten, that's ten steps of rework versus one — and the tokens are the smaller half of that, because the wall-clock is what breaks an SLA.

The boundary rule, stated precisely. Checkpoint after a side effect completes, never before. If the checkpoint lands first and the process dies mid-write, resume replays a write that may already have happened. Combined with idempotency keys derived from run and step, this makes replay safe — which is the pairing that matters, because either alone leaves a duplicate-effect window.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

flowchart TD
    A["🔁 A step completes"] --> B{"🔀 Did it cause<br/>a side effect?"}
    B -->|"yes"| C(["💾 Checkpoint now — always"])
    B -->|"no"| D{"🔀 Would redoing it<br/>be expensive?"}
    D -->|"yes"| E(["💾 Checkpoint"])
    D -->|"no"| F(["⏭️ Skip — let resume redo it"])
    C --> G{"🔀 Is anything in state<br/>re-derivable?"}
    E --> G
    G -->|"yes"| H(["📎 Store a reference, not the artifact"])
    G -->|"no"| I(["✅ Write full state"])

    style A fill:#D1D5DB,stroke:#9CA3AF,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style B fill:#C4B5FD,stroke:#8B5CF6,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style D fill:#C4B5FD,stroke:#8B5CF6,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style G fill:#C4B5FD,stroke:#8B5CF6,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style C fill:#6EE7B7,stroke:#34D399,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style E fill:#6EE7B7,stroke:#34D399,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style F fill:#93C5FD,stroke:#60A5FA,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style H fill:#FCD34D,stroke:#F59E0B,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style I fill:#6EE7B7,stroke:#34D399,color:#000000,font-weight:bold

The second question is the one that keeps checkpoints small. A retrieved document, a large tool result, a generated file — all re-derivable or externally stored, so the checkpoint carries an identifier and the restore path fetches. What must be in the checkpoint is the decisions: the plan, the step index, what has already been done.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "After a deploy, three customers were charged twice."

Root cause. The agent checkpointed before executing each step, so state recorded "about to charge" rather than "charged". A rolling deploy evicted workers mid-run, resume read the last checkpoint, and re-executed the charge — which had already succeeded at the provider. The charge tool had no idempotency key, so the provider had no way to recognise the retry. Each individual mechanism was reasonable: checkpointing was on, resume worked, the deploy was routine. The composition was wrong.

Fix. The checkpoint moved to after the effect, and write tools took an idempotency key derived from run id plus step index so a replay collapses at the provider. Both were needed — moving the checkpoint alone still leaves a window between the effect completing and the write landing, and the key alone doesn't stop the agent from deciding to do it again.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

You said this is a workflow-engine problem. Why does that framing matter?

Because it stops the conversation inventing new answers to a solved problem. Durable execution — checkpoint, resume, replay, compensation — has been engineering practice in workflow engines for years, and the agent case adds nothing structurally new. Temporal, Step Functions and a graph framework's checkpointer are all doing the same thing.

Saying it also sets the right expectations about cost. Durability isn't free in any of those systems either — you pay in write latency and state-schema discipline — so the trade is familiar rather than surprising.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Checkpointing every step adds a write to the hot path. When is that not worth it?

When the run is short enough that redoing it is cheaper than the accumulated write cost. For a three-step run finishing in two seconds, a crash costs a retry the user won't notice, and per-step writes are pure overhead.

The threshold I'd reason about is whether a crash is recoverable invisibly. If yes — nothing external happened and the user just waits — skip it. Once a run has side effects or takes long enough that a user notices the restart, the write cost is buying something real.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

The state schema has to change and there are in-flight runs checkpointed under the old one. What now?

This is the part people don't plan for, and it's the ordinary schema-migration problem with a twist: the rows are paused programs rather than records. So the restore path has to be version-aware — read the checkpoint's schema version and upcast old shapes to the current one, which means every schema change needs a migration function rather than just a new field.

The practical discipline is additive-only changes wherever possible, and a deprecation window measured against your longest realistic run. If runs can pause for days at an approval gate, that window is days, which makes the schema effectively a public API with a compatibility policy. I'd also drain or fail-forward deliberately at deploy time rather than letting the two coexist by accident.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design durable execution for a platform where agents run from seconds to weeks.

I'd separate the run's control state from its data, because they have different lifetimes and different access patterns. Control state — plan, step index, pending approvals — is small, written per step, and read on resume. Data — documents, tool outputs, generated artifacts — goes to an object store with references in the checkpoint, so checkpoint size stays roughly constant regardless of how much material a run touches.

For the weeks-long case the binding constraint isn't storage, it's schema stability and external validity. A run paused for three weeks may resume into a world where its tool credentials expired, the target record changed, or the approval it's waiting on is no longer meaningful. So resume needs a revalidation step rather than a blind continue — check that preconditions still hold, and fail into a human path if they don't.

Operationally I'd want run age and paused-run count as first-class metrics, because a run paused indefinitely is invisible otherwise, and the cost of that invisibility is what the §7 human-as-a-tool failure story is about.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "We use a framework with a checkpointer, so durability is handled."

✅ Reality: The checkpointer gives you the mechanism. What goes in the checkpoint, where the boundaries fall relative to side effects, and how the schema evolves are all yours — and those are where duplicate charges come from.

❌ Trap: "Checkpoint before the step so you know what you were about to do."

✅ Reality: That's precisely the double-execution shape. Checkpoint after the effect completes, and pair it with an idempotency key so a replay collapses. Intent is useful for debugging and belongs in the trace, not in the resume point.

❌ Trap: "The checkpoint is our audit log."

✅ Reality: They have different readers, retentions and shapes. Checkpoints are overwritten and sized for resume; audit records are append-only and sized for compliance. Conflating them gives you an audit trail that loses history and a checkpoint that's too big to write per step.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • Durable Execution — Checkpointing, HITL Interrupts, Time Travel — the mechanism.

  • statefulness and persistence — where state lives.

  • HLD reference index §18, §60 — idempotency keys and exactly-once effects, which this pairs with.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §7 Partial completion & orphaned effects — checkpoint placement is half of that solution.

  • §7 HITL as a durable pause — a pause is a checkpoint that waits.

  • §5 Which store holds this state — checkpoint contents are that decision's thread-state branch.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Back-office workflow automation — multi-day runs make this the spine.

  • §14 Support agent that takes actions — the double-charge failure story is its core risk.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Saga — compensating transactions when there's no distributed transaction to roll back — Pattern: Saga (microservices.io)

  • Transactional outbox — the only correct way to update the DB and publish atomically — Pattern: Transactional outbox (microservices.io)

  • Idempotency keys, and storing the first result per key including failures — Stripe API: idempotent requests

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • statefulness and persistence — agent state and persistence.

  • HLD reference index §29 (Saga), §30 (Outbox & CDC), §18 and §60 (idempotency, exactly-once effects) — the patterns in their original form.

What this note adds: the mapping. These are ordinary distributed-systems patterns and the vault owns them as index lines; nothing owns what changes when the thing orchestrating them is non-deterministic. The short version is that an agent is a saga orchestrator that occasionally chooses differently on replay — which is the part your backend background lets you say and most candidates can't.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The framing that scores? An agent run is a saga. No new physics — saga, outbox, idempotency all apply.
What's different from a normal saga? The orchestrator is non-deterministic; replay may choose a different path.
Why compensation, not rollback? The effects are in other people's systems. There's nothing to roll back.
What outbox buys here? Atomicity between "agent decided" and "effect published".
The invariant to state? Every write step has a compensating action, or it's the last step.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

An agent run that makes several writes is a saga, and I'd say that out loud because it moves the problem onto solved ground. When a run fails halfway you can't roll back — the record was created, the email went out — so you need compensating actions per step, and the design question is what "undo" means for each write. Two things make the agent case different from a textbook saga: the orchestrator is non-deterministic, so a replay may not repeat the same path, and the step boundaries are decided at runtime. Idempotency keys handle the first; recording effects rather than intentions handles the second.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Compensating actions (saga) Multiple writes across systems that must succeed or be undone together. A compensator per write, and compensators can fail too. Create-then-notify-then-update across services.
Outbox A local write and an external effect must be atomic. A relay process and eventual, not immediate, publication. "We updated the DB but the event never went out."
Idempotency keys only Writes are naturally retryable and order doesn't matter. No undo — you can repeat safely but not reverse. Independent writes; failure means "try again later".
Defer all effects to the end The plan can be fully computed before anything is written. Loses adaptivity — you can't react to a write's result. Read-heavy runs with a single write phase.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Saga A compensator per write tool; an undo log in run state. Compensation runs cost real calls on the failure path. Failed compensations need a human queue — they can't be retried forever.
Outbox An outbox table plus a relay; effects publish asynchronously. A relay to run; publication latency. Relay lag becomes a metric; a stalled relay is a silent outage.
Idempotency keys A key derived from run and step; result stored per key. Key store and its TTL. Key collisions and expiry are the failure modes.
Defer to end A two-phase shape: plan and validate, then execute writes. Cheapest — most runs never write. Simplest to operate; the constraint is on what the agent can do.

The redraw test: a saga puts an undo log in run state and a compensator beside each write tool. An outbox puts a table and a relay in the picture. If the diagram shows writes with no undo path and no outbox, the failure mode is "half-done and silent".

5. 🔢 The Numbers

Why rollback isn't available. The agent's writes land in systems you don't control — a payment provider, a mail service, a partner API. There is no distributed transaction spanning them, so the only mechanism is a compensating action: refund the charge, send a correction, revert the record. This is exactly the saga argument, and it's why "we'll wrap it in a transaction" is the wrong answer in an agent round.

The two-generals problem the outbox solves. Updating your database and calling an external service are two operations with no atomicity between them. Either order fails somewhere: write-then-call loses the effect if the process dies between them; call-then-write loses the record of an effect that happened. The outbox makes the write and the intent-to-publish one local transaction, and a relay does the calling — so the failure window moves to a place where retry is safe.

Where the agent differs from a textbook saga. In a conventional saga the orchestrator is deterministic: replay takes the same path. An agent's orchestrator is a model, so a replay from a checkpoint may decide differently — skip a step it previously took, or take one it previously skipped. That makes the compensation log a record of what actually happened, never of what the plan said should happen. Compensating from the plan is the subtle bug, because the plan and reality diverge precisely in the runs that failed.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

flowchart TD
    A["⚙️ A write step"] --> B{"🔀 Can its effect<br/>be undone?"}
    B -->|"yes"| C["📝 Register a compensator<br/>in the run's undo log"]
    B -->|"no"| D{"🔀 Can it be deferred<br/>to the end?"}
    D -->|"yes"| E(["⏭️ Move it after all reversible steps"])
    D -->|"no"| F(["⏸️ Gate it — a human approves before it runs"])
    C --> G{"🔀 Is a local write paired<br/>with an external call?"}
    G -->|"yes"| H(["📤 Outbox — one local txn, relay publishes"])
    G -->|"no"| I(["🔑 Idempotency key from run + step"])

    style A fill:#D1D5DB,stroke:#9CA3AF,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style B fill:#C4B5FD,stroke:#8B5CF6,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style D fill:#C4B5FD,stroke:#8B5CF6,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style G fill:#C4B5FD,stroke:#8B5CF6,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style C fill:#93C5FD,stroke:#60A5FA,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style E fill:#6EE7B7,stroke:#34D399,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style F fill:#FCD34D,stroke:#F59E0B,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style H fill:#6EE7B7,stroke:#34D399,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style I fill:#6EE7B7,stroke:#34D399,color:#000000,font-weight:bold

The ordering move in the middle is worth saying explicitly: put irreversible effects last. A saga whose irreversible step is third has a window where failure leaves you unable to compensate; the same saga with it last fails cleanly, because everything before it can be undone.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "The order was created and the customer never got the confirmation. We only found out when they called."

Root cause. The agent's flow was: create the order in the database, then call the mail service. The process was evicted between the two. The order existed, no email had been sent, and nothing recorded that one was owed — the only trace was a run that stopped mid-way, which no alert was watching because the run hadn't errored, it had simply ceased. On resume the agent read its checkpoint, which said "order created", and moved on to the next thing.

Fix. The outbox pattern: the order insert and a send_confirmation outbox row committed in one local transaction, with a relay publishing to the mail service and retrying until it succeeded. The email became at-least-once with an idempotency key rather than best-effort. The general form — a local write and an external effect need atomicity and you can't get it directly — is the oldest problem in the section, and agents hit it constantly because a run is a long sequence of exactly that pairing.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

Why can't you just wrap the run in a transaction and roll back?

Because the effects aren't in one database. A run creates a record here, charges a provider there, sends mail somewhere else — three systems with no shared transaction manager, and two of them belong to other companies. There's nothing to roll back.

What you have instead is compensation: for each write, a defined action that undoes its business effect. A charge is compensated by a refund, not by a rollback, and the difference matters because the refund is itself a new operation that can fail.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Compensators can fail too. What happens then?

That's the honest limit of the pattern, and the answer is a human. A compensation that fails after retries goes to an operations queue with the run's undo log attached, because at that point the system knows what it did and can't fix it — which is exactly the situation a person needs to see rather than a system needs to retry.

What I'd design for is making that state small and legible. The undo log records what actually happened rather than what was planned, so someone picking it up can see "charged £40, refund failed twice" and act. The failure mode to avoid is a compensator retrying forever against a provider that will never accept it, which turns a visible problem into a silent backlog.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

The agent replays from a checkpoint and takes a different path than before. What breaks?

The assumption every conventional saga makes — that replay is deterministic. If the first attempt created a record and the replay decides that step isn't needed, you have an orphaned record with no compensator registered, because the log was built from the plan rather than from events.

The fix is to make the undo log append-only and event-sourced: every completed effect writes an entry at the moment it happens, independent of what the plan says. Then compensation walks the log backwards regardless of what the replay chose to do. It also argues for making the effect log part of durable state rather than reconstructing it from the trace, because the trace is for humans and the log is load-bearing.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design the write path for an agent platform where teams add tools with side effects.

I'd make the compensator a required field on any tool registered as a write — a tool can't ship without declaring how its effect is undone, or declaring explicitly that it can't be, which routes it into the gated-and-last category. That turns a design discipline into a registration constraint, which is the only thing that survives a growing catalogue.

The platform owns the log and the orchestration: every completed effect appends to a per-run log with its key and the arguments needed to compensate, and failure triggers a backward walk the platform executes. Teams supply the compensator; they don't get to implement the saga.

For the local-write-plus-external-effect case I'd provide an outbox as a platform primitive rather than a pattern teams reimplement, because the relay is where the subtle bugs live — ordering, at-least-once delivery, poison messages. What I'd watch is the count of runs in "compensation failed" state, which is the number that tells you whether the design is actually holding.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "Retries handle partial completion — we retry the failed step."

✅ Reality: Retry fixes a step that failed; it does nothing for steps that succeeded before a later one failed. Those effects are still out there. Retry and compensation solve different halves, and a system with only retry leaves half-done runs behind.

❌ Trap: "We compensate by walking the plan backwards."

✅ Reality: The plan is what the agent intended; a non-deterministic replay may have done something else. Compensate from an append-only log of effects that actually completed, or you'll skip an orphan and undo something that never happened.

❌ Trap: "Exactly-once delivery would solve this."

✅ Reality: There's no exactly-once across a network. You get at-least-once delivery plus idempotent effects, which is what the key is for. Saying "exactly-once effects, at-least-once delivery" is the phrasing that shows you know the distinction.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • HLD reference index §29 Saga, §30 Outbox & CDC, §43 delivery semantics — the patterns in their general form.

  • statefulness and persistence — where the undo log lives.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §7 Checkpointing — checkpoint placement relative to effects is the other half of this.

  • §4 Read tools vs write tools — the write lane is exactly the set of steps needing compensators.

  • §1 Autonomy level — an irreversible step with no compensator is one that needs a gate.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Support agent that takes actions — refunds and account changes are the canonical saga.

  • §14 Back-office workflow automation — multi-system writes with compensation is the whole problem.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Interrupts that persist state and resume with a value supplied later — LangGraph: durable execution

  • Human intervention as a designed trigger, not an error path — A practical guide to building agents (OpenAI, PDF)

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • human-in-the-loop — approval gates and where they sit.

  • Durable Execution — Checkpointing, HITL Interrupts, Time Travel — the interrupt mechanism.

What this note adds: what the pause costs in design terms. A wait measured in days is not a longer version of a wait measured in seconds — it forces durability, an expiry policy, and revalidation on resume, because the world moves while the run is stopped.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What a pause must not hold? A process, a connection, or in-memory state.
The three fields of a pause? What's being asked, what resumes it, when it expires.
The default on expiry? Named explicitly — usually deny and escalate. Never "wait forever".
What resume must do first? Revalidate preconditions. The world moved.
The metric that catches the silent failure? Paused-run count and age.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

A human pause is an unbounded wait, so nothing about it can live in memory. The run checkpoints, emits a task carrying what's being asked and what would resume it, and the worker releases — the approval comes back as a payload keyed to the run rather than as a signal to a process. Three things people leave out: an expiry with a named default, revalidation on resume because the world moved while the run was stopped, and a metric on paused-run age, because a stuck pause produces no error and nothing counts it.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Blocking wait in-process Never in production. Demos only. Any restart loses the run silently. A future or a sleep holding run state.
Durable pause + poll The approver checks a queue on their own schedule. Latency until they look; a queue to staff. Internal back-office approvals.
Durable pause + push The approver should be told, and latency matters. Notification delivery, retries, and a channel to maintain. Customer-facing or time-sensitive approvals.
Optimistic execute + compensate Waiting costs more than undoing, and undo is cheap. You have to actually build the compensator. Reversible actions where speed is the product.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
In-process wait Nothing — which is the problem. Holds a worker for the whole wait. Runs vanish on deploy; nothing counts them.
Pause + poll Checkpoint, an approval task store, a resume-with-payload path. Token cost stops during the pause; wall-clock is unbounded. Queue age and SLA become live metrics.
Pause + push All of the above plus a notification path with retries. Delivery infrastructure. Undeliverable notifications become their own backlog.
Execute + compensate No pause at all; an undo path instead. Compensation cost on the reversal path. You'll reverse things in public sometimes.

The redraw test: a durable pause makes the checkpointer mandatory and adds an approval store plus a resume edge. If the diagram shows a human box with a plain arrow and no store, the pause is in memory and the run is a deploy away from disappearing.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

Why the wait's length changes the design rather than the parameters. A second-scale wait can hold a connection; a day-scale wait cannot hold anything — not a process, not a pod, not a database connection. Somewhere between those the design has to change shape, and it's cheaper to assume the long case from the start than to discover it when approvals start taking overnight.

The expiry policy, which is the part that's usually missing. Every pause needs a timeout and a named default. Without one, the failure isn't an error — it's a run that sits indefinitely while the approver is on leave, and it produces no signal at all. The default should be the safe direction, which for an irreversible action means deny and escalate rather than proceed.

Revalidation on resume. A run paused for three days resumes into a changed world: the order may have shipped, the credential may have expired, the customer may have cancelled. So resume is not "continue from step N" but "check the preconditions still hold, then continue" — and when they don't, route to a human rather than proceeding on stale facts. This is the failure mode long pauses introduce that short ones don't have.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

flowchart TD
    A["⏸️ The run needs a human"] --> B{"🔀 Could the wait<br/>exceed a deploy?"}
    B -->|"no"| C(["⏳ A short blocking wait is tolerable"])
    B -->|"yes"| D["💾 Checkpoint and release the worker"]

The first question is the useful one, because "could the wait exceed a deploy" has an honest answer in most organisations and it's usually yes. Once it is, everything else on the diagram is forced.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "An approval sat for nine days and then the agent proceeded with it anyway — on an order that had already been cancelled."

Root cause. Two defects composed. The pause had no expiry, so nothing escalated when the approver was away. And resume was a blind continue from the checkpoint: the agent had captured the order state at pause time, the approval payload said yes, and it executed against facts that were nine days stale. The cancellation had happened on day three, in a different system, which the run never re-read because nothing told it to.

Fix. An expiry with deny-and-escalate as the default, and a revalidation step on resume that re-reads the entities the pending action touches and aborts into a human path on any material change. The general shape: a durable pause is a fork in time, and the longer the fork, the less the state you captured can be trusted.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

Why can't the run just wait? The framework supports long-running executions.

It can wait — but nothing may be held while it does. The distinction matters because "the framework supports it" usually means the framework persists state and releases the worker, which is exactly the design I'm describing. Where teams go wrong is implementing the pause themselves as a blocking call, which works in development and loses runs on every deploy.

The test I'd apply: if every process in the system restarted right now, would the paused run survive and still be resumable? If not, it isn't durable regardless of how long it can wait.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

When is optimistic execution with compensation better than pausing?

When the wait costs more than the undo. A reversible action where speed is the product — provisioning something a user is waiting for, sending a draft they can retract — is often better executed with a short window to cancel than gated behind an approval nobody's watching.

The condition is genuine cheap reversibility, including reputationally. Un-sending an email isn't free even when it's technically possible, because the customer already read it. So the test isn't "can we reverse this" but "is reversing it cheaper than waiting", and for anything customer-visible the answer is usually no.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

Thousands of concurrently paused runs. What breaks?

Not storage — paused runs are small and cheap. What breaks is visibility and the queue. With a handful of pauses someone notices a stuck one; with thousands, a run paused forever is indistinguishable from one paused legitimately, so you need age distribution and per-approver backlog as first-class metrics rather than something you check.

The second thing is approver throughput becoming the system's actual capacity limit. Past a point the answer isn't engineering — it's reducing how many runs need approval, by raising thresholds where the approval rate shows the gate isn't buying anything. A gate approved 99% of the time is latency, not safety, and at thousands of runs that's a large amount of human time spent confirming the expected.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design the approval layer for a platform where many agents pause for many kinds of decision.

I'd make the approval a first-class durable object rather than a message: an id, the run it belongs to, a typed payload describing the decision, the entitlement required to answer it, an expiry, and a default. Agents create them; the platform owns their lifecycle. That way expiry, escalation and audit are implemented once instead of per agent.

Routing is the part that needs designing rather than defaulting. An approval needs to reach someone entitled to answer it, which means the payload carries a required role rather than a named person — people leave, teams reorganise, and a run paused on a departed employee's queue is the stuck-run failure with extra steps.

On the agent side I'd make revalidation mandatory rather than optional: resume calls a precondition hook the tool declared, and a tool with a pending approval has to define one. That converts the stale-facts failure from something each team remembers into something the platform enforces.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "The run waits for the approval — that's what the pause is."

✅ Reality: The run doesn't wait; its state persists and the worker goes away. Anything else holds a process for an unbounded time, and the first deploy during a wait loses it silently.

❌ Trap: "We'll add a timeout later if pauses turn out to be a problem."

✅ Reality: The problem is silent by construction — a stuck pause raises no error and completes no run, so nothing counts it. You discover it when a customer asks, which is the most expensive discovery path available.

❌ Trap: "On resume, continue from where it left off."

✅ Reality: After a long pause the captured state may be stale. Resume has to revalidate the preconditions of the pending action and abort into a human path if they've moved — which is the difference between a pause and a suspension.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • human-in-the-loop — the gate this note makes durable.

  • Durable Execution — Checkpointing, HITL Interrupts, Time Travel — the interrupt primitive.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §7 Checkpointing — a pause is a checkpoint that waits, so durability comes first.

  • §1 Autonomy level — supervised autonomy is implemented as this pause.

  • §4 Human-as-a-tool — the same mechanism seen from the tool layer.

  • §2 Sync vs async runs — any human gate forces the async side of that fork.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Support agent that takes actions — refund approval is the canonical pause.

  • §14 Back-office workflow automation — multi-day HITL checkpoints are the design.

notes.title: What the queue does when it can't keep up

headings.text: ⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)
🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)
🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Accept, enqueue, stateless workers — the async execution shape — LangGraph: durable execution

  • Backpressure and load shedding in their general form — HLD reference index §§ on queueing, backpressure and rate limiting

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • deployment and scaling — the queue-and-worker architecture.

  • concurrency and parallelism — concurrency across a run.

What this note adds: the overload policy, which the architecture note assumes. Agent queues differ from ordinary job queues in one way that matters: the scarce resource is usually provider tokens-per-minute rather than your own compute, so adding workers makes things worse rather than better.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The scarce resource? Provider rate limit, usually — not your CPU.
Why more workers can hurt? They multiply concurrent model calls into the same limit.
The three overload responses? Shed, degrade, or queue — pick deliberately per lane.
What per-tenant limits prevent? One tenant's burst starving everyone else.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

Agent runs are long and bursty, so the queue-and-worker shape is a given. The decision is what happens at capacity, and the thing that catches people is that the binding limit is usually the model provider's tokens-per-minute rather than your own compute — so autoscaling workers makes the queue drain slower, not faster, because they all contend for the same budget. My defaults are per-tenant concurrency caps so one customer can't starve the rest, priority lanes so interactive traffic isn't stuck behind batch, and explicit degradation — fewer sub-agents, smaller models — before shedding.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Queue and wait Async work with generous deadlines. Latency grows unbounded; users see nothing happening. Batch, scheduled, or background runs.
Shed load Interactive traffic where a late answer is worthless. Rejected requests — the user must retry. A human is waiting and a timeout is near.
Degrade Quality is negotiable and an answer beats no answer. A worse result, which you must communicate. Multi-agent runs where breadth can shrink.
Per-tenant fair share Multi-tenant, always. Throughput for the heaviest tenant is capped. One customer's burst affecting others.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Queue A durable queue plus stateless workers. Cheapest; cost is deferred, not reduced. Queue depth and age are the health signals.
Shed Admission control at the gateway with a clear rejection. Rejected work costs nothing. Shed rate becomes a capacity signal you must act on.
Degrade A quality knob the runtime can turn: worker count, model tier. Reduces spend under load — the only option that does. Users need telling; silent degradation erodes trust.
Per-tenant Token buckets per tenant, enforced at the gateway. Predictable per-tenant ceiling. Per-tenant queue metrics; noisy-neighbour complaints stop.

The redraw test: all four live at the gateway and the queue, not inside the agent. If your picture puts overload handling in the loop, it's in the wrong place — by the time the loop sees it, you've already admitted the work.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "We autoscaled to forty workers under load and throughput went down."

Root cause. The queue backed up, the scaling policy saw depth rising and added workers, and every new worker started issuing model calls into the same account-level rate limit. The provider began returning 429s, the harness retried with backoff, and retries consumed more of the limit than the original calls — so useful throughput fell while worker count rose. The autoscaler read the still-growing queue and added more.

Fix. A global concurrency cap derived from the provider's token budget rather than from queue depth, with workers acquiring a lease before starting a run. Queue depth stopped driving scaling, and shedding was added at the gateway so the queue couldn't grow without bound. The general lesson: scale on the resource that's actually scarce, and for agents that's rarely your own compute.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • deployment and scaling — the architecture this note sets policy for.

  • HLD reference index — backpressure, load shedding and rate limiting in general form.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §13 Provider rate limits — the constraint that makes this section necessary.

  • §10 Spend caps — the same gateway, a different budget.

  • §6 Cost & error multiplication — worker count is both a quality and a capacity parameter.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Internal agent platform — per-tenant fairness is the platform's core queueing decision.

  • §14 Deep research agent — parallel workers multiply rate-limit pressure per run.

notes.title: What a cancel actually reaches

headings.text: ⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)
🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)
🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Wall-clock and step budgets as run-level controls — LangGraph: durable execution

  • Idempotency keys, which decide whether a cancelled-then-retried write is safe — Stripe API: idempotent requests

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • reliability engineering — budgets and caps in the reliability context.

  • concurrency and parallelism — in-flight work during a run.

What this note adds: where cancellation actually lands. A cancel that only stops the loop leaves in-flight tool calls running, so the honest question is which effects are still possible after the user has been told it stopped.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What a naive cancel misses? In-flight tool calls — they complete after the loop stops.
The three budgets? Steps, tokens, wall-clock. All three, or the run finds the gap.
What makes cancel safe? Idempotency keys plus a compensator on anything that landed.
Cancel vs timeout? Same mechanism, different trigger. Build one path.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

Cancelling an agent is harder than stopping a loop, because the loop is usually not what's running — a tool call is. If I only set a flag the loop checks between steps, an in-flight write completes after I've told the user it stopped, which is the worst possible outcome. So cancellation has to propagate: a context passed into tool execution, honoured by the HTTP client, with a defined answer for effects that landed anyway. And I set all three budgets — steps, tokens, wall-clock — because a run will otherwise find whichever one I left open.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Cooperative flag between steps Tool calls are fast and side-effect-free. An in-flight call completes regardless. Read-only agents with sub-second tools.
Propagated cancellation Anything with slow or effectful tools. The default. Plumbing a cancellation context through every tool. Tools that take seconds, or that write.
Cancel + compensate Effects may land between the signal and the stop. A compensator per write, and a window you must accept. Irreversible actions mid-run.
No cancellation, budgets only Batch work nobody watches. A user abort does nothing until a budget trips. Scheduled runs with no interactive caller.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Flag A check between steps. Trivial. Nothing saved on the in-flight call. Users see "cancelled" while work continues.
Propagated A cancellation context threaded into every tool and HTTP client. Stops spend at the point of cancel. Cancelled-mid-write becomes a state you must handle.
Cancel + compensate The undo path from §7's saga note, triggered by cancel. Compensation runs cost real calls. Failed compensation after cancel needs a human queue.
Budgets only Three caps in the harness. Bounds the worst case; doesn't respond to a user. Budget-exhaustion rate is the signal.

The redraw test: real cancellation is a signal that reaches the tool layer, so it appears as a path into the boxes that do work. A flag checked in the loop touches nothing outside it.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "The user hit stop, the UI said cancelled, and the ticket was created anyway."

Root cause. Cancellation set a flag the loop checked at the top of each iteration. When the user cancelled, the agent was inside a create_ticket call that took about four seconds. The loop saw the flag after that call returned, reported cancellation, and stopped — by which time the ticket existed. Nothing was wrong with the cancellation logic; it simply operated at a granularity coarser than the thing it needed to stop.

Fix. A cancellation context passed into tool execution and honoured by the HTTP client, so an in-flight request is aborted rather than awaited. For writes that may have landed anyway — the request reached the server before the abort — the run registers the effect in the undo log and compensates, because an aborted client call is not evidence the server didn't act. That last part is the bit that's easy to miss and is exactly the at-least-once problem in a new costume.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • reliability engineering — budgets as reliability controls.

  • HLD reference index §43 — delivery semantics, which is why an aborted call proves nothing.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §7 Partial completion — a cancel mid-write is a partial completion by another name.

  • §8 Hard budgets — the three caps are that section's mechanism, set here.

  • §4 Read tools vs write tools — only the write lane needs the compensating half.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Voice / interview agent — barge-in is cancellation with a sub-second deadline.

  • §14 Deep research agent — long runs make user aborts routine rather than exceptional.

notes.title: Whether to support forking a run from step N

headings.text: ⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)
🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)
🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Time travel — resuming from a prior checkpoint and forking alternate paths — LangGraph: durable execution

  • Replaying recorded tool responses in a controlled environment — Simulation and replay for agent evaluation (Anthropic)

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Durable Execution — Checkpointing, HITL Interrupts, Time Travel — the mechanism.

  • simulation & replay — replay for evaluation.

What this note adds: the constraint that decides whether replay is usable. Replay is only safe when side effects don't re-fire, so supporting it is really a decision about recording tool results — and that recording is the same artifact your eval set wants.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What makes replay unsafe? Side effects re-firing. Replay must read recordings, not call tools.
What you must record? Tool inputs and outputs per step, alongside the checkpoint.
The dual use? The same recording is a replay fixture and an eval case.
What replay can't reproduce? Model non-determinism — a fork may take a different path.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

Forking a run from step N is the most useful debugging tool an agent system can have — change a prompt, replay from the checkpoint, see whether the outcome changes. The constraint is that replay must not re-execute side effects, so it only works if tool results were recorded at the time and the replay reads those instead of calling out. That recording is the real decision, and it pays twice: it's what makes replay safe, and it's exactly what a simulation-based eval needs. What replay won't give you is determinism — the model may choose differently, which is a feature for exploring alternatives and a nuisance for reproducing a bug.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
No replay Short cheap runs; re-running from scratch is fine. Debugging long runs means re-running them. Runs in seconds, no side effects.
Replay with recorded tool results Long or effectful runs; debugging matters. Recording storage, and fixtures that go stale. "What would have happened if the prompt said X?"
Replay against live tools Read-only agents only. Any write re-fires. Never safe otherwise. Pure retrieval with no mutations.
Fork for exploration Comparing alternative paths from a decision point. N× cost per fork; non-determinism muddies comparison. A/B on a prompt change mid-run.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
No replay Nothing. Nothing. Debugging is re-running and hoping it recurs.
Recorded replay Tool results stored per step beside the checkpoint. Storage per run; no model cost until you replay. Recordings go stale as tools change — they need a refresh policy.
Live replay None — and side effects fire again. Full cost per replay. Dangerous for anything but reads.
Forking Branch identity on checkpoints; results compared per branch. One full run per fork. Comparing non-deterministic branches needs several samples.

The redraw test: replay adds a recording store beside the checkpoint store, and a switch in the tool layer between "call" and "read the recording". If there's no switch, replay hits production.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "Someone replayed a failed run to debug it and re-sent the notifications."

Root cause. The framework supported resume from a checkpoint, and a developer used it to investigate a bad outcome. Resume re-executed from the chosen step against live tools, because nothing distinguished "resume this interrupted run" from "replay this completed run for inspection" — they were the same operation. The steps after the fork point included a notification that had already gone out, so customers received it twice, days after the original.

Fix. Replay became a distinct mode with the tool layer switched to recordings, and the resume path gained a guard refusing to resume a run already marked terminal. The distinction that matters: resume continues unfinished work and should hit real tools; replay inspects finished work and must not. Collapsing them into one verb is what caused this.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • Durable Execution — Checkpointing, HITL Interrupts, Time Travel — the mechanism.

  • simulation & replay — the eval use of the same recordings.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §7 Checkpointing — replay forks from a checkpoint, so its granularity sets yours.

  • §12 Simulation & replay — the recordings this produces are that section's fixtures.

  • §4 Read tools vs write tools — only the write lane makes live replay dangerous.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 "Our agent succeeds 60% and costs too much" — replay is how you test a fix without re-running everything.

  • §14 Coding agent — forking from a decision point is the natural debugging loop.
